text: Besides technical knowledge, employers increasingly look for so-called soft skills, such as communication, teamwork and adaptability. This is because technology changes so rapidly that specific knowledge can become outdated within a few years, whereas the ability to learn quickly never does. In the past, loyalty and experience in a single field were prized, but today flexibility is often more valuable.

text: Both have their place. University provides a theoretical foundation and teaches you to think analytically, whereas on-the-job training offers practical experience that is hard to replicate in a classroom. Ideally, the two should be combined, for example through internships. In my view, graduates who have had some work experience are usually better prepared and also find jobs faster.

tips.en: Both have their place accepts the value of both sides.

text: Not necessarily. Although some older workers may need more time to adapt to new technology, they often compensate with experience, patience and a stronger sense of responsibility. The problem is more about attitude and opportunities than age itself. If companies offer regular training and treat learning as a normal part of the job, employees of all ages can keep up.

tips.en: Not necessarily gently challenges a stereotype.
More about … than shows the real cause.
tips.kk: More about … than шын себепті көрсетеді.

text: I'd say routine skills, like data entry or basic translation, will be increasingly automated, so people will need to focus on what machines do poorly, such as creativity, empathy and critical thinking. It's both a threat and an opportunity: those who adapt will become more productive, while others may be left behind. That's why lifelong learning will be essential.
